title: Fast Escape, Slow Convergence: Learning Dynamics of Phase Retrieval under Power-Law Data
claim: Heavier-tailed input spectra sharply slow convergence beyond the exponential decay of the isotropic case, with slowdown growing as the spectral exponent increases.
layout: 1 panel, log-log plot, five colored curves, legend inset at left
description: A single log-log line plot of MSE (y-axis, 10^-4 to 10^0) against training time t (x-axis, 10^3 to 10^7). Five colored curves, one per spectral exponent a (0 blue, 0.5 orange, 0.75 green, 1.25 red, 1.5 purple), are listed in a boxed legend at the left. All curves start on a plateau near MSE 1. They then drop at progressively later times as a grows. The a=0 curve (the isotropic case) falls steeply around 10^5. The a=1.25 curve falls near 10^6 to 10^7. The a=1.5 curve declines only slowly and has not converged by the end. The curves that finish reach a noisy floor near 10^-4. A dotted grid covers the plot. The eye goes first to the steep blue drop and the widening gap between the curves.
caption: Evolution of the MSE during training with online SGD for different spectral exponents \texorpdfstring{\(a\)}{a} (log-log scale). For $a>1$, convergence is markedly slower than the exponential decay seen in the isotropic case, reflecting the difficulty of learning directions associated with small eigenvalues.
abstract: Scaling laws describe how learning performance improves with data, compute, or training time, and have become a central theme in modern deep learning. We study this phenomenon in a canonical nonlinear model: phase retrieval with anisotropic Gaussian inputs whose covariance spectrum follows a power law. Unlike the isotropic case, where dynamics collapse to a two-dimensional system, anisotropy yields a qualitatively new regime in which an infinite hierarchy of coupled equations governs the evolution of the summary statistics. We develop a tractable reduction that reveals a three-phase trajectory: (i) fast escape from low alignment, (ii) slow convergence of the summary statistics, and (iii) spectral-tail learning in low-variance directions. From this decomposition, we derive explicit scaling laws for the mean-squared error, showing how spectral decay dictates convergence times and error curves. Experiments confirm the predicted phases and exponents. These results provide the first rigorous characterization of scaling laws in nonlinear regression with anisotropic data, highlighting how anisotropy reshapes learning dynamics.
